subject: maths
question: If we consider the set of rational numbers and the set of irrational numbers, what elements are present in both sets?
solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

**Rational numbers** (p/q form) and **Irrational numbers** (cannot be p/q) are **mutually exclusive**.

By definition, no number can satisfy both conditions at the same time.

The **intersection** of two disjoint (non-overlapping) sets is always an **empty set**.

**∴ The correct answer is Empty set.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** The set of **Rational numbers** (denoted by Q) and the set of **Irrational numbers** (denoted by I or Q').

**Formula Used:** The **Intersection** of two sets A and B, denoted by A ∩ B, is the set of elements that are in both A and B.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/0f0255f496ef2afd3253fdc85d3e27644d0b374b60bb4524ec2e410abc92bf9d.png] 

⇒ **Rational numbers** are all numbers that can be written in the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0.

⇒ **Irrational numbers** are all real numbers that are **not rational** (cannot be written as p/q).

⇒ Since a number is either rational or irrational, there is no number that is both.

⇒ Therefore, Q ∩ I = ∅ (the **null set** or **empty set**).

**∴ The correct answer is Empty set.**

**__Additional Information__**

Real Number System

The set of **Real numbers** (R) is the union of the set of rational numbers and the set of irrational numbers (R = Q ∪ I).

Decimal Representation

**Rational numbers** have decimal expansions that either terminate or repeat. **Irrational numbers** (like π or √2) have non-terminating and non-repeating decimal expansions.

Disjoint Sets

Two sets are called **disjoint** if they have no elements in common. Their intersection is always the **empty set**, denoted by ∅ or { }.</p
